newsitem.title: CROATIA: Catholic church in Serb-held town bombed.
newsitem.headline: Catholic church in Serb-held town bombed.

text.p: A bomb exploded on Tuesday outside a Roman Catholic church in the Serb-controlled enclave of Eastern Slavonia in Croatia, a United Nations spokeswoman said.

"An explosive device went off at 4 a.m. (0300 gmt). It was placed at the front door of the church. Civilian police were dispatched there this morning," said Kathy Ladun of the U.N. Transitional Authority (UNTAES) in the enclave.
The Croatian news agency Hina, quoting an UNTAES duty police officer, said the explosion left a 80-centimeter (0.8-yard) mark on the bricked front doors of the church in Ilok.
No injuries were reported and there was no indication as to who might have planted the bomb.
The Franciscan Church of St John in Ilok has been damaged three times since 1991 when the area was occupied by local Serb paramilitaries backed by nearby Serbia.

UNTAES, with 5,000 combat-trained peace troops, took charge of Eastern Slavonia a year ago with a mandate to gradually restore Croatian government rule in the region by mid-1997. The area's Serb militia was disbanded by UNTAES last summer.

Ilok, Croatia's easternmost town, witnessed the most recent ethnic violence in the enclave when a Serb mob attacked a group of Croat Catholics bused in by UNTAES from government-run territory to attend a Christmas Eve mass.
Some 100 Serbs massed before the church in Ilok, throwing explosive devices and insulting Croats.
Some 50 Croat refugees from the 1991 war in the region were trapped inside the church for three hours until UNTAES brought in military and civilian police reinforcements.
After the Croats left the church following the mass, Serbs broke into it, smashing windows and damaging the vestry.
Several Croats and UNTAES personnel were attacked, and a U.N. policeman was injured in the disturbance.

Armed minority Serbs seized almost a third of Croatia in a 1991 revolt against its move to independence from Serbian-led Yugoslavia. But the Croatian army retook all rebel lands except Eastern Slavonia in two blitz offensives last year.
Many thousands of the estimated 120,000 Serbs in Eastern Slavonia have now applied for Croatian citizenship papers.

Others remain hostile to Croatian authority and some have demonstrated against the step-by-step reinstatement of Croatian institutions and an increasing number of UNTAES-assisted visits by Croat refugees preparing to resettle in their homes.
